dossiers.title: L.A. Noire
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Crime-scene inspection, gathering physical clues and interrogations that require evidence-backed contradictions are the dominant detective loop; shooting and driving appear in smaller action sequences.
1940s Los Angeles, period vehicles and radio, noir writing and detailed facial animation make investigations and character conversations distinctive strengths.
Question choices sometimes seem to follow a narrow scripted logic even where multiple pieces of evidence would fit; players disagree on whether that is satisfying deduction or guessing.
Cases progress in a fixed procedural order with promotion between departments, mixing repeated clue gathering with varied investigations and action interludes.
Case themes and investigations remain varied for many players, but driving between locations, chases and formulaic investigative steps can feel repetitive over a long run.
The broad city is largely an atmospheric backdrop to tightly authored cases rather than a dense GTA-like sandbox; optional street crimes and collectables provide limited side activities.
The intertwined detective and corruption narrative has memorable characters, but the final stretch or unresolved threads divide players.
Driving and shootouts can feel stiff or routine compared with the more original investigative systems, although the option to let a partner drive eases travel.
Steam players report a 30 FPS cap, occasional visual glitches and third-party launcher or sign-in friction; these are dated player experiences, not proof that all current installations fail.

dossiers.title: Children of Silentown
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Traditional point-and-click inventory puzzles mix with singing-based minigames that reveal memories or hidden thoughts as Lucy investigates her village.
Hand-drawn storybook art, eerie music and a gloomy village atmosphere are major recurring attractions, with several players viewing the mood more as a dark fairytale than conventional horror.
Repeated mazes, cogs, light and singing puzzles eventually dominate the flow for some players, despite initially charming musical mechanics.
A very slow walk speed, item pixel hunting and sometimes opaque progression leave players stuck, often without useful hints.
The story starts with domestic chores before the forest mystery develops; some value its gradual, melancholy pacing while others find the early stretch tedious.
The missing-villagers mystery and symbolic story invite interpretation; opinions diverge over whether the ending is moving or insufficiently explained.
Additional song notes and collectibles expand the puzzle vocabulary, while multiple endings encourage revisiting sections to explore different outcomes.
Single-save and replay restrictions, plus lengthy final puzzles, make collecting other endings or missed achievements annoying for some players.
Russian reviews discuss story and puzzles in Russian, and official Steam metadata currently lists Russian interface and subtitles; no broad translation-quality complaint was established.

dossiers.title: The Story of Henry Bishop
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The short first-person horror adventure combines searching a mansion and neighbouring locations for clues with small item puzzles, key finding, stealth and occasional melee or gun fights.
Gothic rooms, supernatural creatures and a mysterious vanished-family story can create scares, but the narrative's sudden transitions or thin explanations reduce immersion for other players.
Enemy detection, stealth and melee hit registration feel unreliable in several accounts; some players resort to running past monsters or repeat a fight repeatedly.
Players often describe a compact roughly one-to-two-hour main run, with an ending choice offering a small amount of replay rather than a lengthy campaign.
Most item puzzles are considered straightforward, but particular combat encounters and timed escapes can cause disproportionate retries.
Changing monster and environment encounters offers some variation through the short narrative, while limited unique mechanics make replay mainly attractive for the alternative ending.
Some enjoy the voice acting and independent-horror charm despite modest production, whereas others find the environments and supernatural plot conventional.

Russian-speaking players report dated launch crashes and one 2024 issue of unusually high CPU load or temperature when switching on the flashlight; these isolated reports do not confirm a universal current defect.
